newsitem.title: USA: U.S. farmers seen putting spring wheat under loan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farmers seen putting spring wheat under loan.

text.p: Farmers in the northern U.S. Plains will likely put new crop hard red spring wheat under government loan instead of selling it to local elevators as cash prices fall, trade sources said.

"We'd guess between 50 and 60 percent of hard red spring wheat producers in general would put their wheat under loan," said Mike Krueger, vice-president of Agri-Mark Inc, a Fargo, North Dakota, firm that gives marketing advice to farmers.

"I think with prices as low as they are, plus the fact that particularly in the western two-thirds of North Dakota and eastern Montana their yields aren't going to be good, the farmers have got the bin space and prices are low enough for them to look at loan," Krueger added.
The U.S. Farm Services Agency (FSA) sets loan rates for each county, based on this year's national rate of $2.58 per bushel established in the federal farm bill.
For North Dakota, the statewide average loan rate for wheat is $2.60 per bushel. Cash prices in the Red River Valley were $3.58 per bushel with harvest still several weeks away.
FSA loans pay farmers a set price per bushel for up to nine months. Farmers can redeem the wheat at any time by repaying the loan. If they default, FSA keeps the wheat.

Trade sources said loan activity rarely moves futures prices but can send cash basis levels higher. By putting the wheat under loan, farmers decrease the supply on the market, leading elevators to raise bids.
The loans allow farmers to pay off debts without having to sell the wheat during harvest when prices are traditionally low, said Ray Anderson, program specialist with FSA in Montana.
The statewide average loan rate for Montana is $2.49 a bushel, he said.
"We are looking at a potential for increased loan activity," Anderson said. "We're down to $3.00 or less a bushel (cash price). That's probably at least $2.00 a bushel less than it was last year."

One Montana cash merchandiser said farmers were unlikely to sell in the first few weeks of harvest. With abundant on-farm storage space, many farmers will likely store the wheat or put it under loan, the dealer said.

"The consensus in the country is that the farmer is going to put the wheat away," he said. "Whether it's going under loan or just into the bin remains to be seen, but it doesn't look like much of it is going to end up in the elevator, at least not at first."

Another Montana dealer said low protein levels would also encourage farmers to consider government loans. While it is still too early to determine protein levels, the crop has suffered from moisture stress which can cut protein.
"We're bidding around $2.80 for ordinary (low) protein," the dealer said. "The loan rate for our county is around $2.60. They'll probably put it under a nine-month loan program and see what happens."
